 Medium

 Print A woman performs Chhath in Patna Patna : From Bihar ’s riverbanks to the shores of Mauritius, Fiji and Suriname, Chhath has crossed oceans and generations, carrying the faith and cultural memory of millions. Once closely identified with Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, the festival is now observed by Indian communities across the world. A concerted effort is underway to secure a place for it on Unesco’s Intangible Cultural Heritage List. Bihar art and culture minister Pramod Kumar said the govt of India had taken up the nomination through a multi-country approach, acknowledging Chhath as a tradition that transcends borders. The process, initiated in 2025, involves Mauritius, Suriname, Fiji, the Netherlands and the UAE. The final decision is expected in Dec 2027. The nomination dossier captures the festival’s four-day rituals, traditional offerings, folk songs, history and social significance. It also underlines its environment-friendly practices and the spirit of equality and collective participation at its heart. Kumar said Chhath held a special place among the Indian diaspora, particularly descendants of ‘Girmitiya’ workers who carried the tradition overseas during the colonial period. Unesco recognition, he said, would bring Bihar’s cultural heritage to a wider international audience. The push for recognition has also gathered momentum on the ground. Intach Patna Chapter has been working towards this goal since 2024. Its convenor, Bhairab Lal Das, said the organisation had taken up several initiatives to document the festival’s many dimensions. In collaboration with the Federation of Indian Photography, Intach organised a national photography salon, inviting photographers from India and abroad to capture Chhath celebrations. An international symposium at Buddha Smriti Park Museum in Patna in October 2025 brought scholars together to explore the festival through history, health, psychology, anthropology, environment, folklore and religious studies. The documentation effort also includes traditional Chhath songs in Maithili, Magahi, Bhojpuri, Bajjika, Angika and Surjapuri, as well as a survey of ‘Surya’ idols across Bihar. Join conversation

 Intach’s ‘arghya’ exhibitions in Patna and New Delhi showcased more than 100 artworks rooted in Bihar’s traditional forms, including Madhubani, Manjusha, Tikuli, Patna Kalam and Sujni. Das said the organisation would continue its research, photography and documentation, while engaging scholars and younger generations. The larger ambition is to present Chhath as more than a religious observance: a living tradition connecting communities across continents.
